sections.title: Identification
sections.text: Cortinarius rubellus has a dry, matt, finely fibrillose orange-brown to rusty-brown cap, usually 3–8 cm wide, bell-shaped to convex and often with a conspicuous pointed central umbo. The margin is incurved when young. Relatively distant, notched or narrowly attached gills become reddish to rusty brown. Its slender ochre-brown stem is often a little wider low down and shows broken yellowish bands of veil material, especially below the middle; a delicate pale cortina may be seen only on young specimens. Flesh is pale yellow. Odour may be faintly radish-like or indistinct. The spore print is rust brown.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: An ectomycorrhizal woodland fungus, frequently found among moss in humus-rich spruce woods, sometimes in pine or broadleaf woods. Norwegian records peak in August and September, but local seasons vary. Damp acidic conifer woodland is common habitat, not an exclusive identification test.

sections.title: Similar species
sections.text: The equally poisonous Cortinarius orellanus is usually less sharply umbonate and more often associated with broadleaf woodland. Other orange-brown Cortinarius species can resemble either one. Chanterelles have blunt folds rather than true gills; this difference matters, but should not be used alone to approve a foraged specimen. Yellow veil bands and the fragile cortina may be faint or lost with age.

sections.title: Orellanine poisoning
sections.text: Orellanine can cause severe kidney injury after a long latent period. Early gastrointestinal signs may be absent; thirst, nausea, fatigue, back pain and changes in urine output can begin days after the meal. The Belgian Poison Centre reports kidney symptoms from roughly two to twenty days after orellanine-containing webcaps. A Swedish follow-up of 28 C. rubellus patients found that 22 initially needed dialysis and many later received a kidney transplant; these figures describe that case series, not the risk for every ingestion. Suspected exposure needs urgent medical assessment before symptoms appear.

traits: Dry rusty orange-brown fibrillose cap, bell-shaped to convex with pointed umbo
Relatively spaced, notched to narrowly attached reddish-brown gills
Slender ochre-brown stem with broken yellow veil bands; delicate cortina when young
Pale yellow flesh; radish-like odour possible but not constant
Often in mossy spruce woodland, chiefly late summer to autumn
safetyNote: Potentially deadly kidney poison: never eat Cortinarius rubellus. Orellanine may cause kidney failure after several symptom-free days; lack of early illness is no reassurance. Seek urgent poison-centre or emergency advice after suspected ingestion.
